strengths: The work is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than an Algorithms/General paper: its main value is the unification of eight staged fall datasets, a common ten-class taxonomy, standardized cross-subject/cross-view splits, and an in-the-wild OOPS-Fall evaluation protocol. Under that lens, the problem is important and the benchmark could be useful for the fall-detection community.

The paper clearly motivates a real deployment gap: most existing video fall-detection results are based on staged, controlled environments, while medically relevant systems need robustness to genuine falls and sustained fallen states.
The unified taxonomy is sensible and more clinically relevant than binary fall/non-fall labels because it separates transient actions from static states such as fallen, sitting, lying, and standing.

The benchmark covers a nontrivial amount of data for this niche domain, including 14 hours of unique staged recordings, 42 hours of multiview footage, 101 subjects, and 29 camera views, and the paper documents the constituent datasets and split construction reasonably well.

The empirical analysis is useful as a benchmark baseline: frozen I3D and VideoMAE variants, domain-distance visualizations, classification metrics, and MS-TCN++ segmentation results consistently show that in-distribution performance does not imply in-the-wild robustness.
The paper includes meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussion, especially around demographic bias, privacy, surveillance concerns, and false alarms.
weaknesses: The benchmark’s practical value depends heavily on release quality, but the manuscript does not provide a functioning code/data/annotation link in the main text; the page shows placeholders such as “OmniFall:” and “Code:”. For a dataset/benchmark paper, this is a major reproducibility concern.

The OOPS-Fall construction is under-specified. The paper says it curates 1.3k fall/no-fall segments from OOPS via filtering, manual verification, and annotation, but does not give enough detail on class counts, selection criteria, annotator protocol, agreement, quality control, split definitions, segment duration distribution, or whether ambiguous accidents were excluded.

The staged-to-wild evaluation has a label-space mismatch: staged data uses a ten-class temporal taxonomy, while OOPS-Fall appears to be binary fall/no-fall. This is acceptable for a specific protocol, but the paper does not fully analyze how this mismatch affects conclusions about fallen-state detection, segmentation, or real deployment utility.

The experimental baselines are limited. Frozen feature extractors with a lightweight temporal transformer are useful diagnostics, but the paper does not compare against representative fall-detection methods, modern video classifiers fine-tuned end-to-end, domain adaptation methods, pose-based baselines, or privacy-preserving alternatives. This makes it hard to know whether the reported staged-to-wild gap is intrinsic to the benchmark or partly due to baseline choice.

Some split definitions are debatable for the claimed evaluation axes. For example, cross-view splits for datasets without true synchronized views are approximated using rooms/locations or subject-location changes, and single-view datasets only participate in training for cross-view evaluation. These choices may be reasonable, but they complicate interpretation of “cross-view” results.

The domain-shift analysis is suggestive but not very rigorous. FVD and embedding plots are computed from the same families of pretrained features later used for evaluation, and the paper makes fairly strong interpretive claims about why I3D generalizes better without deeper evidence or ablations.

Important benchmark details appear to be deferred to supplementary material, including additional backbones and numerical FVD values. The main paper would benefit from more complete reporting of the OOPS-Fall statistics and annotation protocol rather than additional qualitative embedding figures.

The writing is generally understandable but has several polish issues and inconsistencies, e.g. typos such as “excempt,” “from from,” “accross,” inconsistent naming of VideoMAE-Pre/VMAE-K400-Pre, and table/figure references that sometimes make the narrative harder to follow.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-served problem: evaluating fall detection under realistic staged-to-wild domain shift, with explicit attention to the clinically relevant fallen state rather than only the transient fall event.

As a Dataset/Benchmark contribution, the idea of unifying several public fall datasets under a common temporal taxonomy and adding an in-the-wild OOPS-Fall evaluation split is potentially useful to the community.

The manuscript includes multiple evaluation views: cross-subject, cross-view, staged-to-wild testing, feature-space distance/visualization, clip classification, and temporal segmentation. The reported OOPS-Fall performance gap is a useful empirical signal.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is not documented rigorously enough for a dataset paper. The manuscript does not provide sufficient detail on annotation protocol, annotator training, quality control, inter-annotator agreement, temporal boundary rules, or how inconsistent source labels were mapped into the ten-class taxonomy.

OOPS-Fall is central to the claimed contribution but is under-specified. The paper only states that 1.3k fall/no-fall segments were filtered and manually verified from OOPS; it lacks class counts, selection criteria, segment duration statistics, examples of rejected cases, train/val/test details, and evidence that these are representative of real-world fall scenarios.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract/page header has blank placeholders for benchmark/code links, and many key numbers are deferred to an unspecified supplement. It is unclear whether videos can be redistributed, whether only annotations are released, and how licensing/consent is handled across the eight public datasets and OOPS-derived clips.

The experimental baselines are too limited for the claims. Using frozen I3D/VideoMAE features plus a lightweight classifier is informative, but the paper does not compare with established fall-detection methods, modern video models fine-tuned end-to-end, domain adaptation baselines, or simpler pose/skeleton baselines that are highly relevant for fall detection.

Several splits are questionable or confounded. Some datasets have extremely few subjects, MCFD has a single subject and is excluded from cross-subject testing, CaucaFall is only used for training in cross-view evaluation, and some cross-view splits also change location/subject. This makes it hard to interpret whether failures are due to viewpoint, subject, background, or dataset identity.

The evaluation reporting is incomplete and sometimes confusing. OOPS-Fall entries in Tables 2 and 3 contain only three unlabeled numbers, the ten-class setup does not directly apply to OOPS-Fall, no confidence intervals or statistical variation are reported, and class imbalance effects remain difficult to assess despite the use of balanced metrics.

The domain-shift analysis is mostly qualitative. FVD heatmaps and t-SNE/H-NNE plots support the broad observation that datasets cluster by domain, but the paper does not provide enough numerical analysis or actionable insight to substantiate stronger claims about why I3D generalizes better.

The writing and presentation need substantial polish. There are typographical errors, inconsistent dataset names, incomplete references, missing years/venues in several citations, and some overclaimed phrases such as the first rigorous staged-to-wild protocol without enough evidence of exhaustive comparison to prior real-world fall benchmarks.

Overall, the paper has a valuable benchmark idea, but the current manuscript does not yet provide the level of dataset documentation, reproducibility, baseline strength, or experimental rigor expected for acceptance at ECCV.

strengths: Although no explicit contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than an Algorithms/General paper; under that lens, the main contribution is significant: it unifies eight public staged fall datasets into a common 10-class taxonomy, supplies standardized cross-subject and cross-view protocols, and adds an in-the-wild OOPS-Fall evaluation target.

The benchmark addresses a real and well-motivated gap in video-based fall detection: prior datasets are small, staged, inconsistently annotated, and hard to compare. The distinction between transient fall actions and sustained fallen states is especially valuable for the medical use case described in the introduction.

The experimental evidence is appropriate for a benchmark paper. The authors evaluate multiple frozen video representations, report cross-subject/cross-view behavior, include binary fall/fallen metrics, provide timeline segmentation results, and analyze domain shift using FVD and embedding visualizations. These experiments support the central claim that staged performance does not reliably predict in-the-wild robustness.

The paper is generally clear and practically useful. Dataset tables, split definitions, label taxonomy, and per-dataset results make the benchmark understandable, and the limitations/societal-impact section appropriately acknowledges privacy, demographic bias, and deployment risks.

The finding that I3D generalizes better to OOPS-Fall despite weaker in-domain accuracy is interesting and potentially useful for the community, because it cautions against relying only on stronger in-distribution action-recognition backbones for safety-critical fall detection.
weaknesses: Reproducibility and release details are not fully convincing in the manuscript. The first page contains placeholders for OmniFall and Code links, but the visible text does not provide actual URLs; for a benchmark paper, the availability of annotations, split files, preprocessing scripts, and licensing instructions is central to the contribution.

The OOPS-Fall construction is underspecified. The paper says it curates 1.3k fall/no-fall segments from OOPS via tag filtering and manual verification, but gives limited detail on class balance, annotation protocol, annotator agreement, segment boundaries, failure cases, or whether these clips truly match the elder-care fall scenarios motivating the work.

The benchmark inherits substantial biases from the source datasets: most staged datasets involve young/healthy actors, controlled rooms, safety props, few subjects in several datasets, and uneven dataset sizes. The paper acknowledges this, but the experimental protocol may still be dominated by CMDFall and UP-Fall despite weighting, and the smaller datasets provide limited statistical confidence.

The staged-to-wild evaluation is important but narrow: OOPS-Fall appears to be used only as a test set with binary labels, so it does not validate the full 10-class taxonomy in the wild or support adaptation/validation studies. This limits how far the paper can claim real-world readiness.

Some methodological choices need stronger justification or ablation, including the fixed 18-token feature sequences, frozen-backbone setup, capped dataset oversampling at 20, and the interpretation that I3D's simpler feature space explains better OOD sensitivity. These are plausible but not fully established.

The paper would benefit from clearer statistical reporting, such as confidence intervals or variance across seeds, especially because several datasets are very small and some reported per-dataset metrics may be sensitive to split choices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served benchmark problem: fall detection models are commonly evaluated on small staged datasets, while real deployment requires robust recognition of both transient falls and sustained fallen states under uncontrolled conditions.

OmniFall is valuable as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: it harmonizes eight existing staged datasets, adds dense frame-level annotations in a 16-class taxonomy, defines cross-subject/cross-view protocols, and introduces a curated in-the-wild test set from genuine accident videos.

The benchmark design is thoughtful in separating staged, synthetic, and in-the-wild domains, enabling controlled staged-to-wild and synthetic-to-wild generalization experiments rather than only in-domain accuracy reporting.

The synthetic component is unusually systematic: prompts vary age, body type, skin tone, ethnicity, environment, camera position, and action-specific details, and the paper includes cross-age and cross-BMI evaluations that begin to probe demographic robustness.

The experimental suite is reasonably broad for a benchmark paper, including domain-shift analysis, video classification with VideoMAE, supervised timeline segmentation with ASQuery, and unsupervised segmentation baselines in the appendix.
The paper includes useful limitations and societal-impact discussion, especially around privacy, surveillance concerns, human-in-the-loop deployment, and possible generator bias.
weaknesses: The declared contribution type is not explicit; I assess it as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper. Under that standard, the central issue is dataset validity and reproducibility rather than algorithmic novelty. The paper is promising, but several benchmark-quality details remain underspecified.

Dataset release is not yet verifiable: the paper says code and datasets will be public upon acceptance, and the project page in the abstract is blank. For a benchmark submission whose main value is reuse, lack of an accessible release, annotation files, prompts, split files, and licensing package at review time is a significant weakness.

The in-the-wild benchmark is curated from OOPS rather than newly collected, and the paper should more carefully justify the claim of being the first public in-the-wild fall benchmark. It is unclear how many OOPS clips were screened, what filtering criteria were used beyond tagged falls, how ambiguous accidents were handled, and whether the resulting set has selection biases inherited from OOPS.

Annotation quality is described only qualitatively. The paper mentions around 10 annotators and two-pass review, but provides no inter-annotator agreement, boundary tolerance analysis, audit sample accuracy, adjudication statistics, or per-class ambiguity rates. This is important because the benchmark’s main contribution is dense frame-level labeling across heterogeneous sources.

Some headline numbers and terminology are confusing: the abstract says 80 hours / 15k videos, the main text also emphasizes 33 hours single-view and 82 hours including multi-view, while contributions mention over 60 hours of manual frame-level annotations. The distinction between recordings, views, unique duration, multi-view duration, and manually annotated versus transferred labels needs to be clearer.

The synthetic-data claim is interesting but somewhat overstated. Synthetic-only classification improves OF-ItW Fall F1 over OF-Staged by only a few points for one backbone, combined training improves only marginally, and timeline segmentation results are mixed: synthetic helps SigLIP2 but hurts I3D on OF-ItW. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical testing are reported.

The synthetic dataset may contain generator artifacts and prompt-induced biases, but the paper does not provide a rigorous quality assessment of generated videos, failure rates, discarded samples, realism ratings, or checks for physically implausible falls. This limits confidence in conclusions about synthetic data surpassing staged real footage.

Cross-view and multi-view protocols may contain easier correlations than implied, because synchronized views can share the same event, actor, environment, and temporal labels across train/test cameras. This is acceptable for view generalization but should be clearly separated from event-level generalization and discussed as a limitation.

The experimental baselines are adequate for demonstrating benchmark use, but not comprehensive. The paper does not compare against specialized fall-detection methods, skeleton/pose-based approaches, multimodal baselines available in some source datasets, or modern video foundation models beyond the selected backbones.

Reproducibility details are partial: implementation hyperparameters are provided, but exact preprocessing, clip sampling, class balancing, thresholding for binary Fall/Fallen metrics, train/val/test file lists, and generated-video prompts/seeds must be released for the results to be independently reproduced.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-standardized problem: robust fall and fallen-state recognition across staged, synthetic, and real accident videos. Framing this as a dense timeline benchmark rather than only clip-level fall/no-fall classification is valuable.

The contribution is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper. Under that lens, the strongest aspect is the attempt to harmonize eight existing staged datasets with a 16-class frame-level taxonomy, cross-subject/cross-view splits, and a test-only in-the-wild target.

The benchmark design exposes a real and useful phenomenon: high in-domain performance on staged data does not translate cleanly to in-the-wild performance. The reported staged-to-wild and synthetic-to-wild comparisons could be useful for future work on domain generalization.

The appendix gives nontrivial detail about source dataset permissions, synthetic prompt construction, split definitions, annotation workflow, feature extraction, and computational resources. The paper also includes meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussion around surveillance, privacy, and synthetic-data bias.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not fully support the paper's strongest claims. The headline conclusion that synthetic data can surpass real staged data is based on modest gains on OF-ItW Fall F1, while 16-class balanced accuracy on OF-ItW remains very low, Fallen F1 is weak, and timeline segmentation performance in the wild remains poor. This makes the practical significance less convincing than the abstract suggests.

The in-the-wild benchmark is relatively small and narrowly sourced: 818 videos / 2.65 hours curated from OOPS. Since OOPS is an existing dataset and not specifically an elder-care fall dataset, the claim of a broad real-world benchmark for deployment-relevant fall detection feels overstated without deeper characterization of scenarios, demographics, camera types, severity, and annotation ambiguity.

Dataset quality evidence is incomplete. The paper describes a two-pass annotation workflow but does not report inter-annotator agreement, boundary consistency statistics, error audits, or independent validation of the 16-class labels. For a benchmark paper with dense frame-level annotations, this is a significant omission.

The synthetic component is ambitious but under-validated. The videos are generated by Wan 2.2 from prompts, yet the paper provides limited evidence that generated falls are physically plausible, demographically faithful, or free from generator artifacts that models could exploit. Cross-attribute results already show degradation for toddlers/elderly/obese groups, but this is not analyzed deeply.

Baselines are limited for a benchmark paper. Classification relies mainly on VideoMAE-K400-style fine-tuning, and segmentation uses ASQuery with a small set of feature choices. There is little comparison to recent fall-detection methods, domain generalization/adaptation methods, or strong video foundation-model baselines, so it is hard to know whether the benchmark conclusions are method-dependent.

Some protocol choices may confound the conclusions. OF-Syn appears closer to OF-ItW partly because both contain many 'other'/outside activities, and the paper itself notes synthetic videos are temporally simpler than staged videos. The analysis does not sufficiently disentangle label distribution, temporal complexity, scene context, and true fall-motion transfer.

Reproducibility and accessibility remain conditional: code and datasets are promised upon acceptance, and several source datasets use noncommercial licenses or author permissions. This may limit the benchmark's practical openness and long-term reproducibility.

The manuscript has clarity and presentation issues, including awkward formatting, missing project-page URL, inconsistent duration framing (33h single-view vs. 80/82h including multiview), and several overconfident statements relative to the reported numbers. These are not fatal alone, but they reinforce the sense that the submission is not yet mature enough for acceptance.

strengths: The work is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than a standard algorithm paper. Under that lens, the contribution is substantial: OmniFall unifies eight staged fall datasets, adds a curated in-the-wild test set, and contributes a large synthetic component under a common 16-class dense frame-level taxonomy.

The paper addresses a real and important gap in fall detection: existing datasets are small, staged, heterogeneous in labels, and weak for out-of-distribution evaluation. The staged-to-wild and synthetic-to-wild protocols are useful and directly relevant to robust deployment.

The benchmark design is thoughtful. The distinction between transient actions such as fall/lie_down and static states such as fallen/lying is clinically meaningful, especially for long-lie detection, and the support for both video classification and timeline segmentation broadens the utility of the dataset.

The empirical evidence is reasonably strong for a benchmark paper. The authors provide domain-shift analyses, cross-dataset classification experiments, demographic split analysis for synthetic data, and supervised/unsupervised timeline segmentation baselines.

A notable result is that synthetic data performs competitively with or better than staged real data for OF-ItW fall classification, and the combined staged+synthetic setting gives the best fall F1. This is interesting and potentially impactful for privacy-preserving data collection.

The manuscript includes useful implementation and dataset details in the appendix: source dataset permissions/licenses, split definitions, annotation workflow, synthetic prompt construction, feature extraction settings, computational resources, limitations, and societal impact discussion.
weaknesses: The central claim that synthetic data can surpass staged real data is promising but somewhat narrow. For classification it is mainly supported with VideoMAE-K400 fine-tuning, while timeline segmentation gives a more mixed picture: synthetic helps SigLIP2 features but performs worse than staged data with I3D on OF-ItW.

OF-In-the-Wild is curated from OOPS rather than newly collected, is only 2.65 hours, and may not fully represent the elder-care or indoor monitoring scenarios emphasized in the motivation. Its test-only role is useful, but the limited scale and source bias should temper claims about real-world generalization.

The annotation process is described carefully, but there is no reported inter-annotator agreement, boundary uncertainty analysis, or quantitative audit of label consistency. This matters because dense frame-level labels and fine distinctions such as fall versus lie_down are central to the benchmark's value.

Reproducibility depends heavily on future release: the paper states that datasets and resources will be made public upon acceptance. For a benchmark submission, stronger evidence of immediate accessibility, exact licensing constraints, and redistribution feasibility would strengthen confidence.

The synthetic data generation is well documented at the prompt level, but exact regeneration may be difficult because Wan 2.2 generation details, seeds, filtering decisions, and rejected samples are not fully specified. Generator-specific artifacts and demographic representation biases remain possible.

Some claims around privacy-preserving data are slightly overstated. Synthetic data reduces privacy risk, but the benchmark also uses public genuine accident videos, which can raise consent and privacy questions, especially for vulnerable situations.

The experimental baselines are adequate for establishing benchmark utility, but not especially broad. More contemporary video-language or temporal foundation models, domain adaptation baselines, and calibration/false-alarm analysis would make the benchmark's difficulty and practical implications clearer.

The paper has several presentation issues, including cramped tables, extraction-visible spacing/formatting problems, occasional typos, and some inconsistent naming such as OF-Sta/OF-Staged and OOPS/OF-ItW labels in tables. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be cleaned up.
